messages.author: ac859c12d81dd7f6
messages.subject: ggplot2 performance
parts:
I know everyone here's aware of ggplot2 performance issues... I seem
to recall Hadley saying something like there was work going on to
improve speed. Any updates?

In case it'd be helpful, I came across an easy-to-reproduce example
that's particularly slow, IMHO.

x=expand.grid(list(id=1:30,f2=1:5,f3=1:5)) # data frame for 750 rows
x$id = factor(x$id)
x=cbind(x, y=sample(10, 750, replace=TRUE))
ptm <- proc.time()
ggplot(x) + geom_line(aes(x=f2, y=y, group=id, colour=id)) +
facet_grid(id ~ f3)
proc.time() - ptm

# user system elapsed
# 105.75 1.01 132.81

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 performance
parts:
Hi:

Here's my take (Win 7, 64-bit R w/ 8Gb memory):

> system.time(print({ggplot(x) + geom_line(aes(x=f2, y=y, group=id, colour=id)) +
+ facet_grid(id ~ f3)}))
   user  system elapsed
  26.40    0.13   26.63

A more or less equivalent version in lattice is given below.

x$id <- factor(x$id)
library(lattice)
library(latticeExtra)  # needed for the 2D labels

> system.time(print({mykey <- list(space = 'right',
+               title = 'ID',
+               cex.title = 1,
+               text = list(levels(x$id), cex = 0.7),
+               lines = list(lty = 1, col = levels(x$id)) )
+ myxy <- xyplot(y ~ f2 | f3 * id, data = x, type = 'l', groups = id,
+                key = mykey,
+                par.strip.text = list(cex = 0.7),
+                scales = list(cex = 0.7))
+ useOuterStrips(myxy)}) )
   user  system elapsed
   7.28    0.05    7.33

So lattice is a little less than four times as fast as the ggplot version. Which do you think took less time to code? Although there isn't a lot of lattice code here, it's reasonably sophisticated, especially in relation to the corresponding ggplot2 code. The time it takes to program the plot you want needs to be factored into the discussion, too. That being said, both plots look nice, but I would have messed around with the legend a bit in the ggplot2 graph (e.g., add a title, shrink the size of the labels) and fussed with the y-axis labels...such fix-ups would even out the overall timings a bit, I reckon...

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 40c5ae10e483a5c4
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 performance
parts: You are unlikely to get usable data just looking at Intel clock speeds.  Memory access speeds can vary hugely between processor models that have similar clock speeds and depending on the mix of on-chip and off-chip processing, if for example the R code has poor locality of reference or the amount of memory access for data is large, then memory access speeds will be the dominant performance factor.  It would be useful to add in processor age and model to the data collected.

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 performance
parts:
I wonder what is the real goal or question being asked? Are we trying
to get some 'true' estimate of the code's speed, partialing out
'error' due to hardware? Are we hoping to be able to make
recommendations as to what the 'ideal' hardware is or find the
relative contribution of processor frequency vs. memory access speeds,
vs. quantity of memory vs. ...? Will knowing the time it takes to run
code on various hardware configurations help to write faster code? It
seems to me that we have jumped straight to the data collection phase,
without considering the goals and design of our study.

Josh

messages.author: ac859c12d81dd7f6
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 performance
parts:
On Sep 4, 5:11 pm, Joshua Wiley <jwiley.ps...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I wonder what is the real goal or question being asked?

I think the question ought to be regression testing (computer science
regression, not stats regression).
a) what is the performance of ggplot2 on some reproducible tests?
b) when developing new versions of ggplot2, how can we make sure that

messages.subject: RE: ggplot2 performance
parts:
It seems what you need is the difference in time to run the same code in two different versions of ggplot2 - or more appropriately (because the different versions may run on different versions of R or require different versions of dependencies) code that calculates the difference between a ggplot2 plot and the same output using graphics::plot (an intrinsic benchmark) for both versions of ggplot2. So, the difference between differences, right?

I'd be happy to run any such code for any two versions of ggplot2. Does anyone have an example?

Leo
